messages.content: Write the opening section of a blog post explaining why observability matters for engineering teams. Around 250 words.

output:
## You can't debug what you can't see

At 3:14 on a Tuesday morning, checkout starts failing for about one customer in forty. Nothing pages. The error-rate dashboard stays green, because one in forty rounds to zero against a wall of healthy traffic. You find out eleven hours later, from a support ticket written by someone who tried four times and then gave up.

The distance between "the system started misbehaving" and "a human noticed" is what observability collapses. That's not the same job as monitoring. Monitoring answers questions you thought to ask ahead of time: is the disk full, is the queue backing up, did the pod restart again. Good questions. They cover roughly the first year of a system's life. After that the failures get strange, and they live in the seam between a retry policy, a connection pool, and one customer whose payload is 400 times bigger than anyone else's.

Observability is the property that lets you ask a question nobody anticipated and answer it without shipping code. Which requests were slow? Slow in which dependency? For which tenant, on which build, holding which feature flag?

A team with that property debugs an incident in a working session. A team without it debugs by guess-and-redeploy: add a log line, wait for the bug to recur, discover the log line was in the wrong branch, repeat. The second team isn't worse at engineering. They're working blind, and blindness is expensive in a way that never shows up as a line item.

---

253 words, saved at `/tmp/obs.md`. The opening commits to a position (observability ≠ monitoring) rather than defining terms neutrally — say the word if you'd rather it stay vendor-neutral or lead with the definition instead.
